name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Voters in 2 North Dakota counties reject property tax increases
description: Voters in two North Dakota counties Tuesday defeated ballot measures to raise property taxes beyond a 3% cap set by the Legislature last year.  The measures came as an early sign of how some counties have grappled to cover rising costs under the limitation set by the Legislature last year. Divide County asked voters to […]
text:
The Traill County Courthouse in Hillsboro, North Dakota. (Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)Voters in two North Dakota counties Tuesday defeated ballot measures to raise property taxes beyond a 3% cap set by the Legislature last year. 
The measures came as an early sign of how some counties have grappled to cover rising costs under the limitation set by the Legislature last year.
Divide County asked voters to approve an additional 2%, or about $37,800 per year over the next four years to help fund the county’s operations. Voters said “no” by a 53% majority, according to complete but unofficial results. Divide turnout was nearly 58%, well above the barely 40% statewide. 
In Traill County, officials put on a measure of an additional 6.41%, or about $461,000 per year over the next four years, to help fund various services due to increasing costs and hiring competition with nearby Fargo and Grand Forks. Voters shot it down by more than 61%. Traill turnout was about 50%, also above the statewide number.
Additionally, seven county measures for increased mill levies failed around the state; only one passed, said Donnell Preskey, government/public relations specialist for the North Dakota Association of Counties. 
“The economy is a big concern, and I think people are just not wanting any more expenses,” she said.
2 North Dakota counties ask voters to override property tax cap

Divide and Traill county officials previously told the North Dakota Monitor that they would have to make budget cuts if voters rejected the measures. Potential examples include full-time positions moved to part-time, delayed road projects and no salary increases.
For such measures to pass, citizens need to better understand the need for more revenue, Preskey said. Counties will have to prioritize and cut certain things due to their limited revenue, she said.
The 2025 Legislature set the 3% cap on annual property tax increases by local governments as part of an expansion of a primary residence property tax credit. The legislation came months after a 2024 ballot initiative that sought to eliminate assessed-value property taxes and force the state to pick up the tab for billions of dollars in replacement revenue. Voters rejected that measure. 
Many counties have used reserves and/or all or part of the 3% property tax increase allowed by law for their 2026 budget, according to data Preskey presented to lawmakers this year.
The Association of Counties supports exceptions to the 3% cap for counties’ difficult costs of health insurance, elections and jails.
House Finance and Taxation Committee Chairman Craig Headland, R-Montpelier, has said he senses no appetite to increase or eliminate the 3% cap.
Reach North Dakota Monitor reporter Jack Dura at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Pillen eyes 2028 ballot if Nebraska lawmakers again stall on property tax reform
description: LINCOLN — Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen hasn’t budged on his approach to cap local spending and cover K-12 education costs to alleviate property taxes he’s called for in the past four years. But in 2027, Pillen’s second term begins with a more skeptical, divided Legislature to his ideas than before. Though he is adding a backstop: […]
text:
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen hosts a news conference talking about his approach for property taxes ahead of the 2027 legislative session on Nov. 6, 2026, in Lincoln, Nebraska, days after securing reelection for four more years. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen hasn’t budged on his approach to cap local spending and cover K-12 education costs to alleviate property taxes he’s called for in the past four years.
But in 2027, Pillen’s second term begins with a more skeptical, divided Legislature to his ideas than before. Though he is adding a backstop: If the Legislature fails, he’ll go to the 2028 ballot.
“All of us, from the river to Harrison, from Falls City to Chadron, from South Sioux City to Benkelman, we’re all ticked off. It’s got to be fixed,” Pillen said at a 30-minute news conference.
Gov. Jim Pillen is joined by two dozen lawmakers for a news conference at the end of the Legislature’s special session to address property taxes that began almost one month prior. Aug. 20, 2024. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Many of Pillen’s proposals are familiar — capping local property taxes and valuations, having the state take on the operational costs of K-12 schools and encouraging local governments to cut spending to lower property taxes. The governor said Nebraskans “spoke loud and clear” and gave him and other state leaders a “mandate” to “solve the property tax crisis.” 
He said his ideas should receive bipartisan legislative support and that a broadened sales tax base remains a solution, which is “such a no-brainer, it’s unbelievable, such common sense.”
“I believe in it so much that if we don’t get things accomplished in ‘27, our team will be working on taking it to the ballot for ‘28, and we’ll let the people speak,” Pillen said.
Going to the 2028 ballot
As for what going to the 2028 ballot would look like if needed — petitions, a legislative constitutional amendment (which requires 30 votes) or wading into legislative races — Pillen said he could not say. Some Republican lawmakers are proactively raising funds for reelection should they face primary challengers for opposing Pillen’s ideas.
“I don’t have all those specifics worked out in our head, but all I’m telling you is that we’re dead serious about fighting for Nebraskans to solve this property tax crisis,” Pillen said.
Data that Gov. Jim Pillen’s team compiled showing how state property tax relief has affected effective property tax collections over time is projected during a news conference Nov. 6, 2026, in the Nebraska State Capitol in Lincoln, Nebraska. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The governor also could not say exactly what deadline he’s imposing, such as whether it’s early on in the 2027 session, when the session ends in late May or a special session in the summer
Said Pillen, “We’ll just see what the attitude of the new Legislature is.”
“If the Legislature doesn’t want to solve the problem, we’ll get started sooner than later,” Pillen continued. “If they’re open to the conversation, if they’re going to make it a red-blue conversation, we’ll figure that out pretty quickly. It doesn’t take a rocket scientist to know that.”
The governor presented data his team compiled indicating that ongoing property tax relief efforts, including state credits to offset local costs, have turned the tide on property taxes. For property taxes on agricultural land, for instance, Pillen said collections are effectively the same as 2013 levels. For residential property, it’s back to 2021 levels, and for commercial property, taxpayers are paying what they did in 2019.
Eric Underwood of Lincoln, former chair of the Nebraska Republican Party, has outlined a 15-petition effort aimed at the 2028 election, including many on property taxes. 
It’s not yet clear whether Pillen might lend support to Underwood’s proposals.
A changing Legislature
Multiple lawmakers who usually supported Pillen’s ideas, such as broadening sales tax revenue, include term-limited state Sens. Rob Clements of Elmwood, Speaker John Arch of La Vista and Ben Hansen of Blair. Those three Republicans will be succeeded by more skeptical conservatives who have expressed some concern about a tax “shift” or more taxation.
The 2026 candidates for the Nebraska Legislature arranged by district. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The Legislature’s 33-Republican legislative supermajority — the minimum votes needed to overcome a filibuster — is also set to end. State Sen. Merv Riepe of Ralston, a Republican, lost reelection, and two other Omaha-area races could flip blue or purple. State Sen. Brad von Gillern of Elkhorn, Revenue Committee chair, is another Republican who could lose reelection if results hold. He was seen as a frontrunner to succeed Arch as speaker.
Pillen has called for lowering the threshold to end filibusters from 33 to 30. However, a majority of lawmakers, across geography and ideology, have said they’re opposed to the idea.
As he’s done in the past, Pillen said his solution is talking more with lawmakers. He said he and his team will “communicate nonstop.”
“When we can all agree on what a definition of a tax shift is, what the definition of a tax cut is, it starts becoming crystal clear that we’ve been duped by special-interest lobbying groups for 50 years,” Pillen said.
He views sales taxes as the right solution because taxpayers can choose whether to make those purchases, as opposed to mandatory income or property taxes. He noted laundry services and ironing of clothes, for instance, which he said he’s done a few times. He joked that first lady Suzanne Pillen might argue with his ironing a little bit.
“I’ll iron my shirt. I’ll mow my own lawn. I’ll wash my car. I’ll do all the normal things that we used to do,” Pillen said. “That’s not people that are in tough shape. They have that opportunity.”
Yet for multiple years, Pillen has tried to rally lawmakers behind his cause. The needle hasn’t moved to push it over the edge of narrow defeats multiple times over.
2026 special session?
Multiple returning lawmakers and lobbyists have questioned whether Pillen might pursue a special session in the next two months, possibly with a more favorable Legislature. Some have wondered whether Pillen might try to cut spending, and some lawmakers have speculated whether legislators could pause lowering income tax rates before it lowers to 3.99% in January.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen hosts a news conference talking about his approach for property taxes ahead of the 2027 legislative session on Nov. 6, 2026, in Lincoln, Nebraska, days after securing reelection for four more years. At right is a map the governor said shows the “mandate” he and other state leaders have to act based on unofficial election results and margins between Republicans and Democrats. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
“Anything could be possible” in a special session, Pillen said, though he said he has not talked to any lawmakers as he’s “worked my brains out” running the state and running for reelection.
“I gave up speculation a long time ago because it almost broke me trying to speculate markets,” Pillen said.
Pillen called a special session in the summer of 2024 solely on property taxes.
However, multiple state senators and lobbyists the Nebraska Examiner has spoken to for months have said few ideas might have 33 votes to pass in 2026, let alone before a new Legislature with more than a dozen fresh faces coming in at voters’ wishes on Jan. 6.
Balancing Nebraska’s budget
Largely absent from Friday’s news conference was talk about Nebraska’s budget, likely in part because Pillen denies that Nebraska is in a “budget crisis.” Some Republicans, such as former state Sen. Julie Slama of Dunbar, have broken from Pillen and called it a “crisis.”
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen talks with reporters after declaring victory in his reelection bid to lead the Cornhusker State on Nov. 4, 2026, in Lincoln, Nebraska. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Through mid-2029, Nebraska faces a budget deficit that could grow as high as $1.2 billion.
“Those numbers over three years are not near as complicated,” Pillen told reporters.
Pillen said he held a cabinet meeting Friday and spent a couple of minutes celebrating cultural improvements and the work that’s already been done. He said the expectation across the Executive Branch is that agency heads will be in the office, rolling up their sleeves and finding efficiencies, such as cutting out “silly things” happening in government.
“Really, really crystal clear: Pleased but sure as heck not satisfied,” Pillen said of his cabinet.
The Legislature convenes Jan. 6. Pillen’s next four-year term begins the next day.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC’s new constitutional amendments pose financial dilemmas for state, local lawmakers
description: North Carolina voters who delivered a blue wave for Democrats Tuesday also overwhelmingly approved two constitutional amendments that will impact taxes for years to come. The first amendment, approved by 62% of voters, caps state income tax rates for individuals and corporations at 3.5%. The second amendment, which 60% of voters approved, requires the state [...]
text:
North Carolina voters overwhelmingly passed three constitutional amendments on Nov. 3, 2026 to authorize lawmakers to impose limits on local governments’ power to raise property taxes, cap the state income tax, and require photo ID for all voters — not just those voting in person. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline) North Carolina voters who delivered a blue wave for Democrats Tuesday also overwhelmingly approved two constitutional amendments that will impact taxes for years to come.
The first amendment, approved by 62% of voters, caps state income tax rates for individuals and corporations at 3.5%. The second amendment, which 60% of voters approved, requires the state legislature to limit increases in local property taxes, reducing the money communities can raise for schools, infrastructure and other needs.
Alexandra Sirota (Photo: NC Budget & Tax Center)
Alexandra Sirota, director of the North Carolina Budget & Tax Center, said Wednesday that the outcome of the constitutional amendments was deeply disappointing for the future of the state.
“We know that people were voting out of concern for rising costs, and we know that one of the best ways for our state leaders to address those rising costs is to fund programs and services that make life more affordable,” said Sirota. “Unfortunately, the tax amendments that passed put in place real limits on future policymakers’ ability to adjust their revenue to the needs of the moment.”
Sirota said the amendments don’t alter the need for increased investments in childcare, housing, and transportation infrastructure. The property tax measure also doesn’t offer any specifics about how the limit should work.
“It really is going to be up to state legislators to craft the exact language and the exact limit that they want to place on local governments,” Sirota said.
 Amendments could hamstring local governments 
Sirota said the proposed property tax limit could affect communities’ ability to upgrade infrastructure through future bonds, fill the gap when the federal government cuts food assistance, or put more money into public education.
This week the State Board of Education released a new report that detailed $18 billion in school facility needs over the next five years for the state’s 115 school systems.
Local governments often use property taxes to fund school capital projects. The newly passed constitutional amendment could limit that.
“What’s most important in this policy development is going to be having the time to really carefully consider how this gets implemented so that local governments are able to keep up with the rising costs they’re being asked to take on,” said Sirota.
New leadership, new ideas 
Rep. Deb Butler, D-New Hanover, said there’s no doubt that the amendments will present new challenges for legislators who now have to decide  how to structure limits on local property taxes without adversely affecting local government services.
Rep. Deb Butler, D-New Hanover (Photo: NCGA)
“Those are going to be some constraints that we’re going to have to work within,” Butler told NC Newsline.
Butler is a senior member of the House Finance Committee who has expressed interest in taking the reins of the committee when Democrats take control of the House in January.
“That’s of course the decision of the Speaker,” said Butler. “But I’ve been working on some ideas about how we generate more revenue, how we get rid of some of these ‘favorite son’ exemptions and how we level the playing field with corporations.”
Butler said the key will be to find a way to create new revenue for North Carolina without hurting small businesses or individual taxpayers.
 Limiting state revenue growth 
Under the state income tax amendment voters approved, the state’s maximum income tax rate is 3.5%. North Carolina’s personal income tax rate currently stands at 3.99%. It’s slated to fall to 3.49% in January, and fall again to 3.24% in 2030 .
North Carolina’s current corporate income tax rate of 2% is scheduled to reach zero by 2030.
The Budget & Tax Center says that as soon as 2028, the state is projected to face real financial challenges if the schedule of rate cuts continues.
“I think the biggest thing that state legislators are going to need to do is stop those scheduled rate cuts to make sure we at least hold the line on funding people’s priorities,” Sirota said.
The State Board of Education released a new report this week that detailed $18 billion in school facility needs over the next five years for the state’s 115 school systems. (Image: Adobe Stock)
In the new school facility needs report, the most common justifications reported for future expenditures are to resolve repairs or deferred maintenance. Plumbing, HVAC, and electrical needs account for $2.8 billion or 30% of all reported renovation needs at the state’s existing schools, according to the Department of Public Instruction.
Sirota notes that the failure to keep up with maintenance needs can often result in greater expense for costly HVAC repairs or mold remediation.
“Those costs need to be met with revenue,” said Sirota.
Sirota said difficult choices lie ahead. She says millionaires are already not being asked to pay their fair share. With the new income tax cap, future lawmakers may need to turn to raising sales taxes or fees, which would be a bigger financial burden on middle- and low-income households.
Some Democrats have suggested repealing the state’s opportunity scholarship program as one source of revenue.
The Republican-controlled legislature earmarked $705 million in its most recent budget for the Opportunity Scholarship Program in 2026-27, with plans to increase that appropriation to over $800 million annually by 2030.
Butler said she’ll leave it up to others in her caucus to determine how to deal with vouchers.
“That is a big source of revenue that needs to be reevaluated,” said Butler.
 Luxuries and loopholes 
Butler said there should be some agreement on easy reforms like removing luxury tax caps in North Carolina.
“In North Carolina, you can buy a $100 million dollar aircraft or yacht, and you pay a tax with a cap of $1,500,” said Butler. “That’s just not right.”
Butler said the next legislature should also revisit the “Blue Ridge exemption,” a property tax loophole for affordable housing that is being used by corporate for-profit developers while costing local governments tens of millions of dollars each year.
Bill to close property tax loophole advances in NC House committee

A bill to close that loophole passed the N.C. House in May, only to languish in the Senate.
“I think there’s a better, fairer way to do that that would generate revenue,” she said.
Butler said as a minority member, she’s had plenty of time to ruminate on some ideas. With a new House Speaker and a new crop of incoming lawmakers, she’s hoping for time to discuss them.
“If I’ve learned anything watching these current leaders, it’s that you don’t do anything in a rushed fashion,” said Butler. “I think about HB2 or the classroom size bill, or any number of things that they’ve gone after at breakneck speed.”
“I’d rather get it right the first time,” Butler said. “These are big changes and you don’t want to do anything that’s going to have unintended consequences.”
